subject: unicornFoal
pitch: A newborn unicorn foal on wobbly long legs. A pearly white coat with a soft lilac shimmer, a short fluffy mane and tail in pastel pink, mint and lavender, a small spiralled horn in gold, big dark eyes with long lashes, little silver hooves, and a daisy chain hanging around its neck.
reasoning:
I need to work within the agentic-3js-builder SDK's constraints, using only the documented API surface for creating builders and joints, since I don't have full docs beyond the reference—just the core functions like createBuilder and joint with their parameters for positioning and hierarchy.

There's a lot more of this API surface I'm cataloging — spike, extrude, lathe, stick, sprout, cards, ring, pose, surface with its nearest/around/ray/scatter/loop/drape methods, decal, membrane, region, along, plus the ik limb function, paint/texture helpers, rng, and the geometric primitives like frame, line, aim, arc, bezier, catmull. Since the exact signatures for things like paint and cards aren't fully specified, I'm leaning toward being pragmatic and sticking to the core API I'm confident about, since the module needs to actually run without errors.

Given the uncertainty around paint/spots/svg/cards/decal signatures, I'm deciding to favor plain color strings for the "wow" factor instead — a pearly white coat with lilac shimmer achieved through a secondary material color, and pastel mane/tail tufts built from small stuck ellipsoids or spike rods in pink, mint, and lavender rather than risking unknown card/texture calls.

For the horn, I'm considering a manually computed spiral path of points fed into a sweep call with a thin radius and gold color to get that spiral taper effect. For the eyes, I'm weighing sphere-based parts for the big dark eyes against using ring or along calls with callbacks to place lash geometry along a curve, though I'm unsure exactly how those callback signatures pass frame data.

Actually, it's safer to skip ring/along entirely and just use explicit point loops with b.part, placing geometry via plain coordinates and aim vectors so pieces attach to the nearest bone automatically without needing an explicit bone reference.

Scale probably accepts a 3-value array or vector. Given the API uncertainty, I'll lean on the most documented functions: createBuilder, joint, chain, sweep, part, stick, surface, extrude, lathe, membrane, rng, frame, line.

Now I'm sketching the actual foal design: a newborn foal roughly 0.85-1m tall, stylized with chunky proportions and long wobbly legs, hooves resting at y=0, facing +Z, with a skeleton built from a hip root through a spine chain to chest, neck, and head.

I'm working out leg joint heights (hoof, pastern, fetlock, knee, elbow) and body/head proportions in meters, aiming for long, slightly splayed, bent-kneed legs typical of a newborn foal, and I'm deciding whether to use a limb/IK helper or build legs manually as a hip-knee-ankle-hoof joint chain.

I'm weighing different API approaches for constructing the legs — chains with named joints versus explicit joint definitions paired with sweeps along point paths — trying to figure out how bone attachment works when a sweep path has no associated joint names.

I'm uncertain how radius variation and chain joint APIs actually work, so I'll lean toward safer primitives — using constant-radius sweeps or basic ellipsoid/cylinder parts via b.part to build the stylized puppet body instead of relying on unverified loft/station fields.

Now I'm sketching the skeleton hierarchy: a root "hips" joint positioned at the rump, then a "spine" chain running forward through a sequence of points toward the withers to form the torso.

For the body itself I'm weighing a swept tube versus separate ellipsoid volumes for the barrel, rump, and chest, leaning toward using overlapping ellipsoids and sweeps together since the stylized foal look doesn't need perfectly seamless connections.

I'm then planning the neck as its own chain running from the chest up to a head-base point, with a separate "head" joint and a distinct "jaw" joint so the mouth can open, keeping the head proportionally oversized for a chibi foal aesthetic.

Now I'm sketching the neck chain path and head placement, uncertain whether the chain API accepts a role option alongside the path, but I'll pass it in anyway assuming unknown properties are tolerated at runtime, then move to defining each leg as its own chain running from hip through knee, fetlock, and down to the hoof.

For a wobbly foal look I'm splaying the legs slightly outward at the bottom while bending the hindlimb hock backward, naming the four leg chains foreL, foreR, hindL, hindR since I can't directly control the auto-generated joint names within each chain, accepting that limitation rather than fighting it.

For hooves I'll attach small cylinder or box geometry near each leg's terminal joint in a silvery tone, letting the nearest-bone logic naturally bind them to the lower leg segment so they move correctly with the chain.

I'll sweep each leg chain with a constant radius for a stylized wobbly-foal look, maybe thinning slightly from top to bottom, and plan hooves at the chain joints with knees bent slightly forward. For the coat, I'll use a pearl-white base with a lilac shimmer layered on top, possibly as a subtly larger semi-transparent overlay to suggest the shimmer effect.

Since I don't know the exact signatures for helper functions like countershade, paint, spots, or stripes, I'll skip those entirely to avoid runtime errors and instead achieve texture through careful color composition. For the mane and tail, I'm planning a fluffy pastel look built from clusters of small spheres or ellipsoids in randomized pastel shades, arranged along the neck ridge from poll to withers.

To keep placement consistent, I'm writing my own math helpers—plain JS functions for interpolation and cubic Bezier curves—rather than relying on uncertain SDK functions, using simple number arrays as point paths.

For chains I'll sample a few points directly from these cubic curves (around 4 per chain) to stay under the joint limit, and reuse the same sampled neck points for positioning the mane puffs so everything lines up. Now I'm working out concrete coordinates and scale, starting from a model height of about 0.95m to the ears.

I'm sketching out joint positions for a newborn foal's legs and body, placing hooves at ground level and defining shoulder, knee, fetlock, and hoof points for front legs with a wobbly bent-knee look, then mirroring for the opposite side, and doing similarly for hind legs with hock and stifle points before setting barrel, withers, and belly heights for the torso.

Now I'm shaping the barrel, chest, and rump as ellipsoids with specific sizes and positions to keep the blocky puppet style, then working out the neck as a curved path of control points rising from the chest toward the head, trying to get the head height proportionate rather than too tall.

I'm still working through how to attach the head joint to the end of the neck chain, considering whether to parent it directly to hips or figure out how to reference the chain's final joint object.

I realize the chain's joint positions just need to visually meet the head joint since the hips remain the single root, so I'll parent head directly to hips and trust the skin geometry lines up at that shared location. I'm unsure exactly how `b.chain` parents its first joint internally, so I may need to pass an explicit `parent` option to be safe.

Given this uncertainty, I decide the safer path is favoring whatever API shape is most likely to actually run: using `b.chain(name, path)` with just two arguments as the cheat sheet describes, and figuring out role assignment separately rather than guessing extra parameters that might throw.

For parenting, I plan to have chains start exactly at points that coincide with existing joints I've already created, so the nearest-joint logic (if that's how it works) attaches them sensibly — like starting the neck chain right at the chest joint's coordinates. I'm aware this might create duplicate joints, but that seems like an acceptable tradeoff given everything else I'm unsure about.

I'm settling on a plausible API pattern: creating a builder, defining a root hips joint, then building chains for the spine and legs off nearby anchor points, letting the SDK handle exact parenting since I can't be certain of the details.

For the jaw and head, I'll place the jaw as a child joint of the head, then use an explicit `bone:` reference when placing mouth parts so they attach to the jaw or head directly rather than relying on nearest-bone inference, since explicit bone assignment should always take priority.

Now I'm considering whether to use a surface/raycast-style API to place small stuck-on details versus just computing part positions directly—since the guidance discourages hand-tuned surface offsets, I'm leaning toward relying on direct position placement with explicit bone references rather than fiddly surface queries.

I'll compute surface points directly using ellipsoid parametric equations (center plus radii scaled by spherical angles), then place eye spheres centered right at that surface point so they protrude naturally rather than relying on arbitrary offsets.

Now I'm sketching the head geometry: a skull ellipsoid, a tapered muzzle ellipsoid forward and down, a smaller jaw ellipsoid, and cone-shaped ears placed upright at the top-back of the head since I can't be sure how to orient them to aim outward without knowing the geometry's default axis.

Then I realize I can bake rotations directly into each geometry using three.js methods like rotateZ before passing it to the part builder, which solves the ear-tilt problem cleanly and means I can construct any shape with translate/rotate/scale and just use `at` for placement. I'm also noting I could use SphereGeometry with scaling instead of a built-in scale option for the ellipsoid shapes, since that approach feels more certain and consistent with how positions are determined by bounding-box centers.

For the mane, I'm thinking of using small icosahedron puffs in pastel pink, mint, and lavender clustered along the neck and tail to create a fluffy foal look, with maybe 25 puffs for the mane and 14 for the tail, picking colors randomly from a small palette. The tail itself would be a short curved chain with a thin core and puff clusters layered along it for a cosmetic fluffy effect.

I'm working out the neck centreline math so I can place mane puffs along its dorsal (top-back) side: sampling the bezier curve, computing the tangent, then deriving a perpendicular dorsal normal in the YZ plane so puffs sit on top and slightly behind the neck surface at the right radius, spread across a few rows with slight left-right offsets for width.

Now I'm adding a forelock tuft between the ears on the forehead, then figuring out the horn: placing its base near the front of the skull and its tip forward and up, and considering how to build a spiral gold horn shape — either as a tube swept along a helical path with shrinking radius, or as a cone with carved spiral grooves.

Since manually orienting a cone geometry would require quaternion math that's disallowed, I'm settling on building the horn as a sweep along helix path points that twist around the base-to-tip axis, letting the sweep function handle orientation naturally.

I'll make the core a plain gold cylinder sweep and add a thinner helix tube over it for the spiral ridges, using a darker gold for the ridges against a lighter gold core. I'll check that sweeping with just two points still works fine for straight segments, and that the helix tube radius staying constant near the tip looks reasonable even as the core tapers to a point.

For attaching the horn, I'll just skip the bone parameter since it's undocumented and let it default to nearest-bone attachment at the head. For the eyes, I'm computing surface positions on the skull ellipsoid so each eye sits roughly on the lateral surface — picking an offset like [0.085, 0.01, 0.06] from the skull center and verifying it lands close to the ellipsoid surface using the standard ellipsoid equation.

I'm giving each eye a protruding sphere (radius ~0.028-0.03) in dark color, plus a small white highlight sphere offset slightly outward along a normal direction so it sits on the eye's surface rather than buried inside. For eyelashes, I'm planning thin tapered sweeps arranged in an arc along the upper eyelid, several per eye, each angled outward.

Working out lash positioning geometry...

For the hooves, I'm planning silver-grey cylinders tapering slightly, placed at the top of each leg's hoof point near the ground.

For the body, I'm settling on a pearly white base with soft lilac shading underneath the barrel to suggest shimmer and dimension, keeping legs white and hooves silver for contrast.

For the mane and tail, I'm going pastel: pink, mint, and lavender strands, with hooves placed at ground level so the pony stands flush at y=0.

Now I'm working out the daisy chain necklace—a looped garland of small white daisies with yellow centers encircling the neck, sagging slightly lower on one side to look like it's hanging naturally.

I'm figuring out how to construct each petal as a small flattened ellipsoid baked with its own rotation and offset, so the daisy forms a disc shape, but orienting the whole flower to face outward from the garland loop still needs a proper rotation to align its local plane with the loop's direction at that point.

I realize I can build an orthonormal basis matrix from my computed tangent/normal/binormal vectors and apply it directly to the geometry, avoiding the usual quaternion-based orientation method and keeping everything as plain transformed geometry positioned at the flower's centre. I'm also considering merging all the petal geometries into one buffer for efficiency rather than adding each as a separate part.

I'll skip the merge utility since it's an extra import that might not be available in the sandbox, and instead just make each petal its own part — a daisy chain of 14 flowers with 7 petals each is around 100 parts, well within budget and triangle limits. Now I'm figuring out the garland shape itself, sweeping flower positions around a closed loop so the daisy chain forms a full ring rather than an open path.

For placement, I want the thin green garland string to sit loosely around the neck, but it needs to avoid colliding visually with the mane crest running along the top of the neck. I'm deciding to position the garland lower, around t≈0.32 along the neck curve, while keeping the mane confined to a higher range starting around t≈0.4, so the two don't overlap awkwardly.

Now I'm working out the precise geometry of the neck's bezier curve, computing its midpoint position and tangent direction to understand how the neck leans and where the garland and head should attach relative to it.

Checking the head placement, I realize the skull radius pushes the top of the head to about 1.1m, which feels too tall for a stylized newborn foal. I'm adjusting the neck endpoint and head center downward slightly to bring the overall height closer to 1.03-1.04m, balancing realism with the chibi proportions.

Now I'm computing the actual neck curve using control points, deriving the midpoint position and tangent vector through the Bezier formula, then setting the neck radius and defining the head skull ellipsoid and muzzle dimensions.

Next I'm placing the jaw and adding a soft pink muzzle patch for a cute detail, then positioning the ears as outward-tilted cones at the top of the skull with a smaller pink inner-ear shape layered on top.

For the eyes, I'm computing surface points on the skull ellipsoid using the normal gradient so the eye spheres sit correctly oriented outward, sizing them generously for a foal-like look, then adding small highlight spheres to give the eyes some life.

I'm layering in iris and pupil spheres that protrude slightly outward from the eye surface for depth, then working out the tangent "up" and lateral vectors at each eye so I can position eyelashes correctly along the upper rim.

Writing eyelash path geometry...

Now I'm working out the horn placement, computing a base point on the forehead and a forward-leaning direction so the horn tip sits above and ahead of the skull, unicorn-style, before moving on to position the ears.

For the horn's structure, I'm considering a stepped-cone approach — three tapering sweep segments shrinking from base to tip — plus a true cone geometry oriented along the horn direction via a custom basis matrix, topped with a spiral ridge wrapped around the surface for a stylized unicorn horn look.

Still writing helix geometry...

The cone needs a tapering radius so the helix tube hugs the cone's surface at 95% of its radius, with gold tones chosen for the horn (lighter gold core, deeper gold ridge). The cone geometry is centered along its axis then oriented and positioned so its base sits on the forehead and the helix wraps toward the tip.

Now I'm moving to the daisy garland, computing a neck point and tangent along a bezier curve to set up the basis for the loop.

For the garland I'm defining a plane perpendicular to the neck tangent, using one axis along the side (x) and the other perpendicular to both the tangent and that axis, so the circular loop sits slightly outside the neck radius with a bit of natural droop at the front.

Now I'm placing twelve daisies evenly around that loop, each facing outward radially from the neck, and starting to build the petal geometry for each flower using small flattened ellipsoid shapes arranged in a ring.

So the daisy's face should point outward along R, meaning its disc lies in the plane spanned by Tt and N, with local z mapping to R. I'll build each flower's geometry in the XY plane with its normal along Z, then apply the basis transform (Tt, N, R) and position it at the computed center point on the garland loop.

Since there's no BufferGeometryUtils merge helper available, I'm weighing whether to just add each petal as a separate part (7 parts per daisy × 12 flowers = 84 parts, which is manageable) or write a small manual merge function that converts indexed geometries to non-indexed and concatenates their position/normal arrays into a single BufferGeometry.

I'll loop through concatenation instead of spreading arrays to avoid stack overflow, so each flower becomes a single merged part—petals plus centre combined, bringing a daisy field down to 14 parts total. For the petal shape, I'm scaling and translating a small sphere geometry to form an elongated, flattened petal then rotating copies around the center to build the full flower.

For the daisy centre I'm adding a small yellow sphere as a separate part since its color differs from the white petals, giving each daisy 2 parts and 28 total for the field. For mane puffs, I'm considering merging icosahedron puffs by colour into fewer parts, but I realize that placing a merged geometry at the origin would attach it to the wrong bone (likely hips instead of neck), so I need to figure out how to keep the mane following the neck joint properly.

Since placing individual puffs near the neck means each one gets attached to the nearest bone segment automatically, I'll keep them as separate parts rather than merging — roughly 30 mane puffs, 20 tail puffs, and 5 forelock puffs total. For the tail, I'm defining a short downward-curving polyline from the hip rear and sampling points along it to place a core sweep plus about 9 decreasing pastel puffs in alternating pink, mint, and lavender for a fluffy foal tail.

Now I'm working out the barrel and rump geometry — placing ellipsoids for the chest, rump, and belly with specific centers and radii so the neck and tail bases sit naturally inside the torso, and reconsidering the lilac belly shading since it would be hidden unless it protrudes slightly or the whole barrel takes on that tint instead.

Rather than countershading the whole barrel, I'm switching to scattering small lilac/mint shimmer flecks as slightly protruding patches across the barrel's surface to create an iridescent effect.

I'm now working through the full head structure — skull, muzzle, jaw, nostrils, pink muzzle blush — then building out eyes with iris, highlights and lashes using computed surface normals, followed by ears with inner pink cones and forelock puffs near the horn base. I'm also planning the mane as rows of soft puff spheres following the neck's dorsal curve in alternating pastel colors, and setting up the tail to be built similarly with puffs sampled along its curve.

Then I turn to the legs: simple radius-constant sweeps ending in small silver cylinder hooves, with the chains possibly splayed slightly outward for a wobbly foal stance. I'm also working out where to place a daisy garland around the neck, computing the tangent-based basis vectors so the loop sits in a plane perpendicular to the neck axis, and figuring out the timing so the garland, mane, and forelock don't overlap awkwardly.

For construction, I'm writing a merge helper that flattens multiple buffer geometries into one combined position/normal buffer, then using sphere and icosahedron primitives scaled into petal and flower shapes, oriented via the neck-tangent basis so each daisy faces outward from the garland loop. I'm also working out the geometry for eyelashes as thin swept tubes anchored to computed tangent/normal vectors at each eye, making sure petal and lash placements don't collide with the muzzle or skull width.

I decide to skip the rng-based randomness entirely in favor of deterministic sine/index-based variation for things like coat flecks, since that avoids uncertainty about the rng API's exact interface while still satisfying the "deterministic build" requirement. I settle on module structure: importing the builder factory and three.js, exporting a meta object and a default build function.

Writing basis and vector helper functions...

I'm defining a horn helix by sampling points along a tapering cone axis with rotating angular offset, then sweeping a thin tube along those points for the ridged unicorn horn, colored in gold tones distinct from the horn's base cone color.

Now I'm laying out the leg chains as coordinate lists for each of the four legs, with forward-bent knees and backward-bent hocks for the hind legs, feeding into constant-radius sweeps for a stylized foal-leg look, then doing the same for the neck chain (sampled from the cubic curve) and the tail chain with its drooping curve and puff positions. I'm sequencing joint creation (hips root, then chest, head, jaw) before building the chains, since each chain should attach to its nearest already-created joint.

I'm now assembling the body parts list -- barrel, chest, rump, and a lilac underbelly ellipsoid -- assigning each to the hips or chest bone, and checking whether the lilac belly's added bulge against the white coat creates an acceptable two-tone banding effect along the torso's sides rather than looking like an odd seam.

I'm scattering small flattened, alternating-colored ellipsoids across the flanks using sine/cosine-based angular placement projected onto the barrel's ellipsoid surface, so they sit as little pearlescent flecks.

I'm detailing the head geometry next: skull, muzzle, a pink blush patch on the muzzle, nostrils, and the two-piece jaw, all parented to the head or jaw bones as appropriate, followed by the ears (outer cones tilted outward plus inner pink cones nested slightly forward) and three small forelock puffs placed between the ears and behind the horn base.

I'm now positioning mane puffs that run along the neck curve using parametric offsets perpendicular to the neck's tangent, varying their size and alternating through pastel colors, and doing the same along the tail's polyline for the tail's puffy sections.

I'm building the floral garland: computing a circular loop around the neck using tangent-derived basis vectors, swept as a thin stem, then placing daisy-like flower clusters and small leaves around that loop using angular offsets, checking that the basis vectors I'm using for orienting each flower's petals face outward correctly by verifying the cross-product handedness with a concrete example.

I'm now checking the overall proportions -- confirming the horn tip height, ear tops, and raised head position are a reasonable scale for a stylized foal, and verifying the neck curve's endpoint tucks correctly into the back of the skull geometry, with everything symmetric about the center axis and the hooves grounded at y=0.

I'm now layering the eye geometry: a dark eyeball sphere, then a violet iris dome offset outward along the eye's outward normal, a black pupil protruding slightly further, and a small highlight sphere, stacking these spherical layers outward from the socket to build up a stylized big-eyed look.
